subject: Vocabulary
description: Common English proverbs + their meanings; SSC PYQ favourites

questions.stem: Meaning of proverb 'A STITCH IN TIME SAVES NINE':

options.option_text: Sewing carefully takes time and effort here
Acting promptly prevents larger trouble later
Wear nine layers of clothing always for warmth
Stitch nine pieces of cloth together as one

questions.explanation: A small + timely action prevents bigger problems later. Origin: small tear in cloth needs only 1 stitch now; left alone, it grows + needs 9. Applies broadly: maintenance > repair, prevention > cure. Common parallel: 'A penny saved is a penny earned'; 'an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure'.

questions.stem: Meaning of proverb 'EMPTY VESSELS MAKE THE MOST NOISE':

options.option_text: Loud places have empty containers
Foolish or shallow people talk most
Quiet people are not knowledgeable
Containers should be filled fully

questions.explanation: Empty / shallow people often boast loudly + show off; truly knowledgeable people are quieter / more humble. Origin: striking an empty pot makes loud sound; a full pot is dull. Comparable: 'Still waters run deep' (quiet people may be deep); 'Half-knowledge is dangerous'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'BIRDS OF A FEATHER FLOCK TOGETHER' means:

options.option_text: Birds need feathers to fly always
People of similar nature stay together
Flocks of birds migrate seasonally
Birds prefer to live in colonies

questions.explanation: People with similar interests, character, or background tend to associate. Used positively or with caution (your friends reflect on you). Origin: birds of same species naturally flock. Compare: 'Tell me your friends, I'll tell you who you are'; 'You are the company you keep'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'A ROLLING STONE GATHERS NO MOSS' means:

options.option_text: Stones are smooth in flowing rivers
Constant change prevents stability + gain
Moss grows only on still surfaces
Stones never accumulate any growth

questions.explanation: Original meaning: a person who keeps changing jobs, places, partners doesn't accumulate wealth, friends, or settled life. Modern usage = sometimes positive (staying free + flexible), but traditionally negative. Origin: ancient Latin (Publius Syrus) — 'Saxum volutum non obducitur musco'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'STRIKE WHILE THE IRON IS HOT' means:

options.option_text: Hit metal only when it's heated
Act when conditions are favourable
Iron is dangerous at high heat
Forge iron tools for daily use

questions.explanation: Take advantage of an opportunity at the right moment. Origin: blacksmith metaphor — iron is malleable only when hot; let it cool + you can't shape it. Modern usage: 'Strike while iron is hot' = act now, opportunity won't last. Similar: 'Make hay while the sun shines'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'WHEN IN ROME, DO AS THE ROMANS DO' means:

options.option_text: Always travel to Rome historically
Adapt to customs of the place you're in
Follow Roman customs strictly always
Romans were the original culture-makers

questions.explanation: When you're in a new place, follow / respect the local customs. Origin: St. Ambrose advised St. Augustine — 'When at Rome, live in Roman style; when elsewhere, live as elsewhere live'. Practical wisdom: cultural sensitivity. Often quoted in business + travel contexts.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'TOO MANY COOKS SPOIL THE BROTH' means:

options.option_text: Cooks need to learn skills more
Excess people in a task ruin it
Broth is hard to make tasty
Cooks should always work alone

questions.explanation: Too many people involved in a single task → confusion + conflicting ideas → poor outcome. Origin: kitchen metaphor — multiple cooks each adding their own thing → spoiled broth. Modern parallels: too many decision-makers, design-by-committee. Counter-proverb: 'Many hands make light work' (when tasks are divisible) — different contexts.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST captures the meaning of the proverb 'DON'T JUDGE A BOOK BY ITS COVER'?

options.option_text: Hard work and perseverance always yield positive results
People who read widely tend to make wiser life decisions
Surface appearances are often deceptive and misleading
Knowledge gained from books surpasses practical experience

questions.explanation: C is correct: the proverb warns against forming opinions based solely on outward looks, as appearances can deceive. Option A is wrong because it relates to effort and reward, not to the danger of judging by appearance.

questions.stem: What does the proverb 'THE GRASS IS ALWAYS GREENER ON THE OTHER SIDE' most accurately mean?

options.option_text: Natural environments are always healthier than urban settings
We consistently find other people's situations more desirable
Travellers who explore widely gain the broadest life perspectives
Agricultural land in hilly regions yields more fertile produce

questions.explanation: B is correct: the proverb means we tend to believe others have it better than us, ignoring our own blessings. Option C is a tempting distractor but it relates to travel and learning, not to envy or dissatisfaction with one's own lot.

questions.stem: Ramesh was lured by a job offer with a flashy salary package. Without deeper research he accepted it, only to find the firm had a toxic culture and zero growth prospects. Which proverb BEST describes his experience?

options.option_text: Fortune favours the brave — bold choices bring rich rewards
Slow and steady wins the race — patience outlasts hasty action
Don't put all eggs in one basket — diversify to reduce risk
All that glitters is not gold — outward appeal can be deceptive

questions.explanation: D is correct: Ramesh was misled by the glittering appearance of the offer without examining its real worth — exactly what 'all that glitters is not gold' warns against. Option C is wrong because the issue is not about risk-diversification but about being deceived by superficial attractiveness.

questions.stem: What does the expression 'IT TAKES TWO TO TANGO' most precisely convey in everyday usage?

options.option_text: The tango dance can only be performed by two trained professionals
A dispute can always be resolved through careful patient negotiation
Both parties in a conflict or situation bear equal responsibility
Success in collaborative ventures demands perfect mutual coordination

questions.explanation: C is correct: the phrase argues that a quarrel or problem involves both sides, not just one. Option D is tempting because it mentions collaboration, but it speaks to coordination for success rather than to shared blame or accountability.

questions.stem: Kavya invested her entire savings in a startup after watching only its promotional video, skipping any background check. She lost everything. Which proverb does her action most clearly VIOLATE?

options.option_text: Look before you leap — weigh consequences before taking action
Every cloud has a silver lining — hope persists even in setbacks
Fortune favours the brave — bold risks often bring great rewards
Necessity is the mother of invention — need drives human creativity

questions.explanation: A is correct: Kavya acted without looking (researching), violating the core wisdom of 'look before you leap.' Option C is a tempting distractor because her investment was a bold act, but 'fortune favours the brave' does not endorse recklessness without due diligence.

questions.stem: Which proverb conveys a meaning most SIMILAR to 'ONCE BITTEN, TWICE SHY'?

options.option_text: Fortune favours the brave — audacity and bold risks yield gains
A burnt child dreads the fire — past hurt instils lasting caution
Barking dogs seldom bite — loud threats rarely lead to real harm
The early bird catches the worm — acting early brings clear advantages

questions.explanation: B is correct: both proverbs express that a bad past experience makes a person wary of repeating it — caution born directly from personal pain. Option C is wrong because 'barking dogs seldom bite' addresses the gap between threats and action, which is unrelated to learning caution from hurt.

questions.stem: The proverb 'THE PROOF OF THE PUDDING IS IN THE EATING' is BEST illustrated by which of the following scenarios?

options.option_text: A chef insists only trained food critics can correctly evaluate cuisine
A recruiter ranks every applicant entirely based on their résumé alone
A critic scores a new film purely on the director's previous reputation
A manager withholds judgment on a new policy until its real results emerge

questions.explanation: D is correct: the proverb means true worth is revealed only through actual experience or tested results, not through theory or reputation. Options B and C are exact opposites — both involve judging before any real experience — making them the most tempting wrong choices.
